Package com.phasmidsoftware.gryphon.java

Class Graph<V>

java.lang.Object
com.phasmidsoftware.gryphon.java.Graph<V>
Type Parameters:
V - the vertex type. Must implement equals and hashCode.
Direct Known Subclasses:
WeightedGraph
public class Graph<V> extends Object
A mutable, lazily-materialised façade over Gryphon's purely functional graph types.

Graph<V> accumulates vertices and edges in ordinary Java collections. When any algorithm is requested, it materialises an immutable Scala graph from those collections, caches it, and delegates to Gryphon's Scala engine. The cache is invalidated whenever the graph is mutated (addEdge(com.phasmidsoftware.gryphon.java.Edge<V>), addVertex(V)), so the Scala graph is always consistent with the Java state.

All BFS and DFS traversals — both Option 1 and Option 3 — delegate to the Scala Visitor engine via JavaFacadeBridge and return a came-from map: for each discovered vertex v, result.get(v) is the vertex from which v was first discovered. The start vertex is absent from the map — it has no predecessor. This is consistent with all other algorithm façades in Gryphon (Dijkstra SPT, Prim/Kruskal MST, Kosaraju SCC).

Path reconstruction: 


 Map<String, String> tree = g.bfs("A");
 List<String> path = new ArrayList<>();
 String v = "D";
 path.add(v);
 while (tree.containsKey(v)) { v = tree.get(v); path.add(0, v); }
 // path == ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

    • inDegree

      public int inDegree(V vertex)
      Returns the in-degree of vertex: the number of edges arriving at it.

      Unlike degree(Object), this works on both kinds of graph. In an undirected graph every edge can be traversed both ways, so the in-degree, the out-degree and the degree are the same number. A self-loop counts once towards each of the in- and out-degrees.

      Parameters:
      vertex - the query vertex.
      Returns:
      the number of edges arriving at vertex.

    • isConnected

      public boolean isConnected()
      Returns whether every vertex is reachable from every other.

      Undirected graphs only, because connectivity of a directed graph has two distinct meanings and neither is assumed: use ConnectedComponents for weak connectivity, treating edges as undirected, or StronglyConnectedComponents.kosaraju(Graph) for strong.

      In Scala this is not declared on a directed graph, so the compiler rejects it. Java cannot express that, so the façade checks and throws instead.

    • bfs

      public Map<V,V> bfs(V start)
      Performs a breadth-first search from start.

      Returns a came-from map; start vertex absent.

      Path reconstruction: walk result.get(v) until the key is absent — that vertex is the start.

      The map records, for each vertex, the vertex it was first seen from. For breadth-first search that is also the vertex it was explored from, so the result is the BFS tree, and walking it back gives a shortest path in edges. Depth-first search is not like this — see dfs(Object).

      The order is not fixed. Adjacency iteration is shuffled, so this may return a different — and equally valid — came-from map each time. If you need one reproducible answer, use bfs(Object, java.util.Random).

      Parameters:
      start - the source vertex.
      Returns:
      the BFS came-from map.

    • bfs

      public Map<V,V> bfs(V start, Random random)
      Performs a breadth-first search from start, drawing its adjacency order from random.

      This is the Java equivalent of putting given Random = Random(42) in scope in Scala. Two calls with generators built from the same seed return the same map.

      Pass the generator rather than a seed so that one generator can span several calls: sharing it across a sequence of traversals makes the whole computation reproducible, which a per-call seed could not express.

      Parameters:
      start - the source vertex.
      random - the generator determining adjacency order.
      Returns:
      the BFS came-from map.

    • dfs

      public Map<V,V> dfs(V start)
      Performs a depth-first search from start.

      Returns a came-from map; start vertex absent.

      This map is not the DFS tree. Like bfs(Object), it records for each vertex the vertex it was first seen from. For BFS that coincides with the vertex it was explored from; for DFS it does not. A vertex can be seen early from one neighbour and then explored later from somewhere deeper, and it is the deeper vertex that would be its parent in the DFS tree.

      The difference is not a corner case. On a graph whose source is adjacent to every other vertex, every vertex is first seen from the source, so this returns a star — whereas the DFS tree of such a graph is a path. Walking the map back from a vertex still yields a genuine path to the start, but not the path the search took. See issue #144.

      The order is not fixed. See bfs(Object); use dfs(Object, java.util.Random) when you need one reproducible answer.

      Parameters:
      start - the source vertex.
      Returns:
      the DFS came-from map — a discovery map, not the DFS tree.

    • dfsAll

      public Map<V,V> dfsAll()
      Performs a depth-first search over every component of the graph.

      dfs(Object) explores only the component containing its start vertex. This method restarts from each vertex not yet discovered, so the came-from map covers the whole graph. Each component's root is absent from the map, just as the start vertex is for a single DFS, so the number of absent vertices is the number of components.

      This javadoc called the result a depth-first forest until #145. It is not one, for the reason given in dfs(Object): the map records where each vertex was first seen rather than where it was explored from, and for depth-first search those differ. It is a discovery map covering every component — which is what you want for counting components or reaching every vertex, and is not what you want if you need the shape of the search itself.

      The order is not fixed. See bfs(Object); use dfsAll(java.util.Random) when you need one reproducible answer.

      Returns:
      the came-from map over all components.

    • bfsUntil

      public Map<V,V> bfsUntil(V start, Predicate<V> goal)
      Performs a breadth-first search from start, stopping as soon as goal holds for a discovered vertex.

      Use this to find a shortest path to a known target without exploring the rest of the graph. The came-from map covers only what was discovered before stopping, so a vertex beyond the goal will be absent.

      Named bfsUntil rather than overloading bfs, because a lambda argument could not then be resolved against the Function<V, Iterable<V>> overload.

      The order is not fixed. See bfs(Object); use bfsUntil(Object, java.util.function.Predicate, java.util.Random) when you need one reproducible answer. This matters more here than elsewhere: which vertices are discovered before the goal is reached depends on the order, so the map's contents can differ between calls, not merely the paths within it.

      Parameters:
      start - the source vertex.
      goal - the stopping condition.
      Returns:
      the partial BFS came-from map.

    • reverse

      public Graph<V> reverse()
      Returns a new directed graph with all edge directions reversed.

      For every edge u → v in this graph, the returned graph contains v → u. The vertex set is preserved. This operation is the first step in Kosaraju's SCC algorithm and is useful for reachability queries in the reverse direction.

      Returns:
      a new Graph<V> with all edges reversed.
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if this graph is undirected.
